newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - US rates, Fed policy seen steady in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US rates, Fed policy seen steady in 1997.

text.p: Modest U.S. economic growth and mild inflation will keep long-term interest rates largely steady and Federal Reserve monetary policy on hold for much of the first half of 1997, said economists in a Reuters poll.

On average, 25 experts surveyed on Monday and Tuesday forecast the 30-year Treasury bond yield would rise to 6.40 percent by January 1 and to 6.51 percent by March 1. They forecast the yield would hold at 6.51 percent through June 1 and dip to 6.45 percent by next December.
In addition, the economists projected on average that the federal funds target rate would not budge from its current 5.25 percent in 1997.

"Balanced economic growth near potential and steady inflation (will) keep the Fed on hold," said Stuart Hoffman, chief economist at PNC Bank Corp. "The economy is not weak enough to get them to ease, but inflation is not enough of a problem to get them to tighten."
Hoffman forecast an easing of credit toward the end of 1997 and a consequent drop in the bond yield to 6.35 percent from 6.50 percent.
"It's not so much we have a big (economic) weakening, but you have a less-than-potential growth path and some of the manufacturing sector is a little weaker," he said.
One variable most respondents isolated was inflation. Even those experts calling for tighter credit said prices appear to be stable and should remain so.

"Inflation as measured currently would be somewhat higher than it is now, but only modestly so on a core basis," said William Griggs, managing director at Griggs & Santow. He projected no change in the short-term fed funds rate in 1997.

And although Charles Lieberman, the chief economist at Chase Securities Inc, called for a series of fed funds hikes next year, he said the speedy economic growth he expects may not produce much inflation.

"I don't think the economy's that weak; the third quarter is an anomaly," Lieberman said. But he added that "I don't know if that actually produces inflation ... (and) I don't think the Fed is going to be particularly preemptive."
Survey respondents calling for higher rates said consumer spending, the largest chunk of Gross Domestic Product, would have to pick up for their projections to pan out.
"At this point the big question mark is consumers," said David Blitzer, vice president and chief economist at Standard & Poor's Corp.

Holiday spending seems to be off to a good start and may be a trend, Blitzer said. "If (consumers) keep spending half as fast as they did the last few days, according to news reports, the economy closes out 1996 with a bang," he said.

Blitzer's bond yield forecast for the beginning of January, at 6.50 percent, was somewhat higher than the average. He projected the yield would rise to 6.65 percent by March 1 and to 6.75 percent by June 1.
